What is a prompt? The 4-part formula for getting the answer you want
Standalone videos Core ideas
Same question, different results
You and a friend ask AI for the same thing. Why does their answer come out great and yours doesn't? The difference is the instruction you type, called a prompt.
What is a prompt?
A prompt is the message you send to AI. Think of AI as a smart assistant who just met you. It doesn't know who you are or what you need yet.
A short prompt makes AI guess
If you only type "write an ad", AI has to guess: what are you selling, to whom, how long should it be? Guessing gives you something generic.
The 4-part formula

The fix is simple: include all four parts. Role: who AI should act as. Context: who you are and who you're writing for. Task: exactly what you need done. Format: how it should look and how long it should be.
Put it into a real prompt
For example: You are an ad copywriter. I sell salted coffee, and my customers are college students. Write a Facebook post introducing our new drink, under 80 words, in a fun tone.
Before and after
Same AI, but this time the answer is ready to use.
Not happy? Just keep chatting
Not quite right? Just send another message: shorter, more fun, add the price. AI will fix it right away.
Try it now: Remember all 4 parts
Next time you ask AI something, remember all four parts. Role, context, task, format. You are ____. I am ____, writing for ____. Please ____. Format it as ____.

What is adaptive learning? Turn AI into your own private tutor
Standalone videos Core ideas
Same lesson, same speed
The whole class learns the same lesson at the same speed. Fast learners get bored, and slower learners fall behind.
What is adaptive learning?
Adaptive learning is when a machine learns how you learn. It's like everyone having a private tutor who teaches exactly where you are.
A 4-step loop
The secret is a loop. The system asks you a question and watches whether you answer right or wrong, fast or slow. Then it guesses your level and picks the next question to match.
Right means harder, wrong means step back
Get it right, and the questions get harder. Get it wrong, and it goes back to the basics you're missing. Words you tend to forget come back just before you would forget them.
You're already using it
Most of the language apps, test-prep apps and vocabulary apps you use run on this loop.
Do it yourself with an AI chat
You don't need a special app. You can turn an AI chat into an adaptive tutor with one message.
Try it now: Turn AI into your tutor

What is LiDAR? How self-driving cars measure distance with light
Standalone videos Core ideas
How does LiDAR work?
In the dark of night, a self-driving car can still clearly see a person walking ahead. The secret is a technology called LiDAR.
Measuring distance with light
LiDAR means measuring distance with light. It's like a bat listening for echoes, but it uses laser pulses instead of sound.
Send a laser flash
Step one: the device sends out a very short laser flash that your eyes can't see. The flash flies out, hits an object and bounces back.
Time the trip there and back
Step two: the device times how long it takes, from sending to receiving. Light is so fast that going 15 meters and back takes only one ten-millionth of a second.
Work out the distance
Step three: work out the distance. Multiply the time by the speed of light, then divide by two, because the light went there and came back.
Millions of dots
The device does this hundreds of thousands of times per second, in every direction. Each measurement is one dot. Together they make a 3D map called a point cloud.
AI reads the point cloud
Then AI reads those dots to tell what is a person, what is a car, and how far away they are. That's how the car knows when to brake.
LiDAR is all around you
LiDAR is also in robot vacuums, mapping drones and the Pro iPhones.
Try it now: Measure height with your phone
Want to try it? Open the Measure app on a Pro iPhone and point it at a person. It will show their height on its own.

Asked AI and still don't get it?
You ask AI about an idea and get a wall of jargon. You read it and still don't understand. You're not slow. AI just doesn't know who you are yet.
AI only adapts when you give it signals
In part 1, we saw that adaptive learning means teaching you exactly where you are. An AI chat can do that, but only if you give it signals. Here are four ways.
Tell AI who you are
One: tell AI who you are, what you already know, and why you're learning. Same question, very different answer.
Let AI test you first
Two: ask AI to quiz you with a few questions before it teaches. It will see where you are, then plan the path.
Still confused? Ask for a new explanation
Three: if you don't get it, don't just reread it. Ask AI to explain it a different way: with everyday examples, comparisons, or as if you were a fifth grader.
Teach it back to AI
Four: explain it back to AI in your own words, and ask it to point out what you got wrong. Your gaps show up fast.
Save notes for next time
One last tip: at the end of a session, ask AI to sum up what you understood and what's still weak. Next time, paste that in, and AI picks up right where you left off.

Why does AI "forget" in long chats?

Standalone videos Core ideas
A call in the middle of the night
Late at night, your child calls, panicking, asking you to send money fast. But it might not be your child.
What is a deepfake?
AI can now copy a person's voice and face. This is called a deepfake.
A few seconds of voice is enough
Scammers only need a few seconds of your voice from a clip you posted online to make new sentences in that same voice. Video calls can have a swapped face too.
Signs to be suspicious

Hang up and call back yourself

Pasting your whole customer file?

Where what you type goes

What is a token? Why AI doesn't read words the way people do
Inside AI's brain · Part 1/8
Opening up AI's brain
You use AI every day, but what is it really doing inside? This eight-part series opens up AI's brain. Part one: AI doesn't read words the way you do.
Scissors that cut sentences
Before it understands anything, AI cuts your sentence into small pieces called tokens. Some pieces are a whole word, some are just part of a word.
Each piece becomes a number
Then each piece is turned into a number. What AI actually sees is a list of numbers, not letters.
Why AI miscounts letters
That's why AI often miscounts letters. It doesn't look at each letter, it looks at whole pieces. Letters hidden inside a piece are easy to miss.
Some languages take more pieces
Languages with accents, like Vietnamese, often get cut into smaller bits than English. The same idea takes more pieces. And how much AI can read, and how much you pay, are both counted in pieces.

What is an embedding? How AI understands word meaning with a map
Inside AI's brain · Part 2/8
So what do the numbers mean?
Last time, we saw AI cut a sentence into pieces and turn them into numbers. So how do those numbers carry meaning? Let's see.
A map of meaning
AI places every word on a giant map. Words with similar meanings sit close together. Cat is next to dog, while truck is far away.
Coordinates are meaning
A word's spot on the map is its meaning, written as a list of numbers. To tell how similar two words are, AI just measures the distance.
Math with meaning
This map can even do math. Take king, subtract man, add woman, and you land very close to queen.
You already use it
You use it every day. Type dog on the beach into your photo app, and the photos show up even though you never named them. The search works by meaning, not exact words.
Try it now: Search photos with words
Open the photo app on your phone and type receipt or birthday cake. And when you ask AI something, just say what you mean. No need to guess keywords.
What about a whole sentence?
But a sentence has a dozen words. AI has to find which words matter, and who "it" refers to. Part three explains that.
bai/21-attention.html
What is attention in AI? Where AI focuses when it reads
Inside AI's brain · Part 3/8
Meaning depends on nearby words
Last time, each word had a spot on the map of meaning. But a word's meaning also depends on the words around it.
The "it" puzzle

Read these two sentences. "The cat didn't jump over the wall because it was too tired." And "because it was too high". You know right away that "it" is the cat in one and the wall in the other. How does AI know?
Threads of attention
The answer is the attention mechanism. Each word "looks" at every other word in the sentence and gives a score: which word matters most to me? Tired goes with cat, high goes with wall.
The whole sentence looks at itself
Every word does this at the same time, repeated across dozens of layers. That's the heart of every chatbot today.
Important lines get buried in the middle
But attention has limits too. When you send a long text, an important line stuck in the middle is easier to miss than one at the start or the end.

Where does AI learn from? Training and AI's knowledge cutoff date
Inside AI's brain · Part 4/8
A brain just put together
We have the machine: cutting into pieces, the map of meaning, attention. But when it's just built, it knows nothing at all.
Reading a whole library
Then people let it read. A huge amount of text: web pages, books, articles, even computer code. More than one person could read in a thousand lifetimes.
Learning by guessing words
The way it learns is simple: hide the next word and make it guess. If it's wrong, it adjusts a little. Repeat billions of times, and it picks up grammar, facts and even how to reason.
The cutoff date
But the reading has to stop on a certain day, called the cutoff date. AI knows nothing about what happened after that day.
What about the latest news?
So if you ask about today's gold price, a new law or this week's news, AI may answer with old information, and still sound very sure.
Try it now: Ask for the cutoff date

How do chatbots learn to answer and say no? From parrot to assistant
Inside AI's brain · Part 5/8
A parrot that only continues
Last time, AI read a whole library. But at that point it's like a parrot: it can only continue sentences, not answer you.
You ask one thing, it says another
Ask it how to sleep better, and it might continue with a list of other questions, because online, questions often sit next to each other like that.
Learning from sample conversations
Next, people write lots of sample conversations: if asked this, answer like that. AI copies them, and starts answering the actual question.
People give scores

Why does AI give different answers to the same question? What temperature is
Inside AI's brain · Part 6/8
Ask twice, get two answers?
Last time, AI learned to answer like an assistant. But ask the same question twice, and you get two different answers. Why?
Scoring a hundred options
Remember: AI guesses the next piece of text. But it doesn't guess just one word. It scores a hundred options. Coffee 40%, bubble tea 25%, and so on.
A prize wheel
Then it draws one based on those odds, like a prize wheel where bigger slices are easier to hit. This time it lands on coffee, next time maybe bubble tea.
The "temperature" knob
This amount of chance has a knob, called temperature. Low temperature: steady, almost the same every time. High temperature: playful and creative, but more likely to drift off topic.
Every word is a new draw
Every word is a new draw. One different word at the start, and the whole rest of the answer goes a different way.

For creative work like naming things or writing slogans, hit regenerate three times and pick the best idea. For work that needs to be exact, like math, ask AI to show its steps and check its own work. Show how you calculated it, step by step, and check your own work.
Your own documents
No matter how well AI guesses, it doesn't know your own contracts or documents. Unless you give them to it. Part seven shows how.

What is RAG? How to let AI read your own documents
Inside AI's brain · Part 7/8
Your own documents

What does AI actually learn?
Everyone says AI is "trained". But when AI learns, what actually changes inside it? The answer: billions of tiny knobs.
Go out for coffee?
Picture a small decision: should I go out for coffee this afternoon? You think about three things: is it raining, did a friend invite you, and do you have money left?
One knob for each thing
Each thing has its own knob, called a weight. A friend's invite pushes hard toward "go", rain pulls the other way. Add them all up, and if it passes a threshold, you decide: go.
An artificial neuron
That is an artificial neuron: it takes a few numbers, multiplies them by weights, adds them up, then decides. Surprisingly simple.
Stacked into layers

Stack thousands of neurons into layers, each layer passing its results to the next, and you have a neural network. The first layer spots lines, the middle layers spot ears and eyes, and the last layer says: cat.
Learning means turning the knobs itself
Big chatbots have hundreds of billions of these knobs, and nobody turns them by hand. "Learning" means the machine turns each knob itself, a little at a time, until it gets the right answer.

Throwing darts
Picture throwing darts at a target. Hitting the bullseye is right. The farther you miss, the more wrong you are. The distance to the bullseye is a number that measures the miss.
A number that measures being wrong
AI works the same way. The machine gives an answer and compares it with the right one. How far off it is becomes a number, called the error, or the loss function.
A photo of a cat
Show the machine a photo of a cat. It says: 70% dog. The loss is very big. Next time it says: 90% cat. The loss is much smaller.
Push the number down
The whole learning process aims at one thing: push this error number as low as possible. Every time it turns the knobs, the machine checks whether the loss went up or down.
You get what you measure
But the machine only optimizes exactly what's measured, nothing more. If essays are graded only by length, it will learn to write long, not better.

How AI learns · Part 3/7
Which way to turn?
Last time: AI measures how wrong it is with a number called the loss. Now the machine needs to know: which way should it turn the knobs to make that number go down?
Blindfolded on a mountain
Picture yourself blindfolded on a foggy mountainside. You want to get down to the valley, but you can't see anything.
Feel with your feet
The only way: feel around with your feet to find where it slopes down the most. Then take a small step that way. Feel again, step again.
Height is the error
For AI, height is the error. Each spot is one way of setting the knobs. Going down means being less wrong. This way of learning is called gradient descent.
Millions of small steps
The machine repeats feeling and stepping many, many times, sometimes millions. Each step turns all the knobs at once, and the error drops a little more.
Long steps or short steps?
Step size matters a lot. Steps too long, and you jump right over the valley and bounce up and down. Steps too short, and you walk forever without getting there.

What is backpropagation? Explained simply
How AI learns · Part 4/7
Which knob caused the mistake?
Last time: AI walks downhill in small steps to reduce the error. But with billions of knobs, how does it know which ones to turn, and by how much?
A bowl of noodle soup sent back
Picture a noodle soup kitchen with three cooks: one makes the broth, one cooks the noodles, one does the seasoning. A customer complains: the soup is too salty.
Trace back through each step
The head chef doesn't scold the whole kitchen. He traces back from the bowl to each step. The heavy-handed seasoner has to change a lot, the noodle cook barely changes at all.
The mistake flows backward
A neural network does exactly that. The mistake at the output is passed back through each layer, from the last layer to the first. This is called backpropagation.
More blame, bigger fix
Connections that caused more of the mistake get turned more, those that caused less get turned less. In a single backward pass, the machine knows how to fix every knob at once.
The foundation of AI
Backpropagation plus gradient descent is the foundation of modern AI. The chatbots you use today were all trained this way.

How does AI hear you?
AI doesn't just read text anymore. It can also hear you talk. You speak into your phone, and the words appear right away. But how does a machine listen?
What is a voice to a machine?
To a machine, a voice is just a list of numbers: how the air vibrates, measured tens of thousands of times per second. Looking at those numbers, it's hard to tell what you said.
Turning sound into a picture
So the machine slices the sound very thin and splits each slice into low and high sounds. Line the slices up, and you get a picture called a spectrogram: bright spots are where there's sound.
Reading the picture into words

Each sound has its own shape: an "ah" is a few horizontal bars, a "sss" is a blur up high. A model that has heard hundreds of thousands of hours of recordings reads those shapes into words, using the meaning of the sentence too.
Noise and people talking over each other
Anything that smudges the picture makes AI mishear. Coffee shop noise blurs the shapes of words. When two people talk at once, their shapes pile on top of each other.
Names are easy to get wrong
AI rarely sees unusual names, so it often guesses a common word instead. A coworker named Leigh might turn into "lay". So always double-check names and numbers.

bai/200-mo-xe-cu-bam-enter.html
What does AI do in the 2 seconds after you press Enter? AI from A to Z
Standalone videos Special episode #200
2 seconds become 10 minutes

You type a question, press Enter, and two seconds later AI answers. This is our two-hundredth special episode, and we'll slow those two seconds down into ten minutes to see what happens inside. Mark's question is very ordinary: is it cold in Hanoi tomorrow, and what should he pack? The moment his finger hits Enter, the clock starts.
The question doesn't travel alone

Stage one, the question doesn't travel alone: before sending, the app packs in the earlier messages of the chat, plus a hidden instruction called the system prompt, written by the app makers, which you never see. All of it together is the context. Remember the desk in video 9 : AI only knows what's on the desk, and can't see anything off it.
Up to the cloud: API, data center

Stage two, up to the cloud: the envelope flies across the internet, through a door called an API, to a data center, buildings full of servers with GPUs, chips built for AI math. At the entrance there are input guardrails that check the question for anything dangerous or sensitive. Mark's weather question passes easily.
Cutting it up: tokens

Stage three, cutting it up: AI doesn't read words the way we do, so the question is cut into small pieces called tokens. Some are whole words, some are half a word or a punctuation mark. Vietnamese, with its accent marks, is usually cut into more pieces than English, so the same idea costs more tokens. Each piece gets a number, like a page number in a very thick dictionary.
The map of meaning: embeddings

Stage four, placing them on a map of meaning: each token is turned into a long list of numbers called an embedding. It works like coordinates on a giant map where words with similar meanings sit close together. On that map, cold sits next to jacket and scarf, and Hanoi sits near Hoan Kiem Lake, the Old Quarter and autumn. That's how AI grasps meaning, not just the letters.
The pieces look at each other: attention

Stage five, the pieces look at each other: this is the most important part, called attention. Each token looks at all the other tokens to find which ones matter most to it. The word for pack in the question pays strong attention to Hanoi and cold, so AI understands Mark needs clothes for a cold trip, not goods to sell. This looking happens again across dozens of layers, each one understanding a bit more. Billions of multiplications run in parallel on GPUs, all in a fraction of a second.
A thinking draft

Stage six, a thinking draft: many models today are reasoning models that write a draft before answering. The draft is very honest: the question needs tomorrow's weather, but the model's knowledge stops when its training ended, so it doesn't know.
Picking up a tool: tool calling

Stage seven, picking up a tool: instead of guessing, AI writes a special request: call the weather tool, place Hanoi, tomorrow. This is called tool calling. Interestingly, AI doesn't run the tool itself: an outside system reads the request, calls the weather service and puts the result on the desk: a cold front tomorrow, 16 to 24 degrees, maybe light rain in the afternoon. Now there's real data on the desk, which is also why AI with search answers questions about today far better than AI without it.
Guessing the first word

Stage eight, guessing the first word: only now does AI start answering, and it answers by guessing. It scores tens of thousands of tokens that could start the reply. "Yes" gets forty percent, "Tomorrow" thirty, "According" fifteen. Then it picks one by those odds, like spinning a prize wheel with big and small slices. This randomness is set by the temperature. Because of this draw, asking the same question twice can give two different answers.
Repeating word by word

Stage nine is repetition until the answer is done. The wheel stops on "Yes", that word is added to the end, and the whole sequence, now one piece longer, runs through all the attention layers again to guess the next piece. Mark's answer is about eighty tokens long, so the whole line runs about eighty times. Each word is sent to the phone as soon as it's ready, called streaming, which is why the answer appears word by word as if someone were typing.
The exit, and where it can go wrong

Stage ten, the exit: before reaching you, the answer passes output guardrails that block harmful content or leaked information. But guardrails can't check whether it's true. Without the weather tool, AI would still guess a sentence that sounds very sure, just not based on real data. That's hallucination, and it comes from the very same word-guessing step.
Back in your hands

The clock stops at two seconds, and the screen shows the answer: a cold front reaches Hanoi tomorrow, it'll be chilly with maybe light rain in the afternoon, so bring a jacket, a scarf and a folding umbrella. Those two seconds held a context envelope, a trip to a data center, a few dozen tokens, dozens of attention layers, one tool call and about eighty word guesses. Every one of those costs electricity and money, which is why free apps usually limit how many messages you can send.
Try it now: 3 things you can do right away

Now that you understand the press of Enter, here are three things you can do right away. One: put enough information on the desk. AI only knows what's in the context, so say who you are, what you need and what result you want. Two: for anything about today, like prices, weather or news, turn on search or check it yourself, because AI without tools only guesses from old memory. Three: if you don't like the answer, ask again or rephrase, because each time is a new draw. If a chat gets too long, start a new one to clear the desk.

The channel's two hundred videos, wrapped up, are this one press of Enter: from tokens and the map of meaning to attention, tool calling and hallucination. Thank you for learning with Mark and Bit for two hundred episodes. Every stage today has its own video.

Bit is off today

Two hundred ninety-nine videos, and it was always Bit teaching and Mark asking. For episode three hundred, Bit takes a day off, and Mark has to handle everything, from waking up to going to bed, using only what he's learned on the channel, while Bit sits and watches with you.
Ten minutes to plan the day

Six-thirty a.m., first thing: Mark's head is full of a dozen jumbled tasks. He dumps them all into the chat, with meeting times and deadlines, and asks AI to put urgent things first and heavy tasks in the morning. Ten minutes later, the whole day fits on one page, and Mark adjusts two spots to suit himself.
A message in the family group

Seven-thirty, the family group lights up with a forwarded message: drinking hot lemon water every morning cures disease for good. Mark doesn't rush to share it; he asks AI where this information comes from, then opens the sources himself. No research says so, so Mark gently replies to the family.
A long email and the weekly report

Nine o'clock at the office, the boss sends a three-page email and wants the weekly report before noon. Mark asks AI to summarize the email into to-dos and deadlines. For the report, he writes a three-part prompt: who he is, what he needs, what format, and attaches last week's report as a sample, so the draft sounds like Mark on the first try.
Almost pasting customer data

Ten-thirty, Mark is about to paste the whole customer list into the chat for AI to sort, then stops: it has real phone numbers and addresses. He deletes the personal details first, replaces them with customer codes, then pastes. The result is the same, and the customers' data never leaves his computer.
A lunchtime headline

Noon, over lunch, Mark scrolls past a headline saying AI will soon replace your job. This morning he saw it clearly: AI does each small task fast, while choosing the tasks, fixing the schedule and keeping customers safe is Mark's part. He reads closely, sees the article rests on one small survey, and calmly keeps eating.
An agent task with guardrails

Two p.m., Mark remembers his mom's birthday is this weekend. He has an AI agent find three gifts under five hundred thousand dong, delivered within two days, with one clear rule: only search and compare, never order or pay on its own. Mark goes back to work and soon gets a neat comparison table.
When AI praises too much

Four o'clock, Mark has an idea for a promotion and asks AI what it thinks. AI showers it with praise, but Mark knows AI tends to agree with whoever asks, called sycophancy, so he asks again: play a tough critic and point out three weaknesses. This time AI names a risk Mark hadn't thought of.
Cooking with what's in the fridge

Six-thirty p.m., home at last, the fridge holds only three eggs, half a bunch of morning glory and a piece of tofu. Mark photographs the fridge and asks AI for a dish for two in twenty minutes. Dinner is garlic morning glory and tofu with egg sauce, no trip to the market.
A call faking his brother's voice

Seven-thirty, the phone rings: Mark's younger brother, panicking, says he's had an accident and needs twenty million dong right away. The voice is identical, but Mark remembers voices can now be faked with deepfakes. He hangs up, calls back on the familiar number, and asks the family password. Turns out his brother is watching football; there's no accident at all.
Helping his niece with homework

Eight-thirty, his little niece asks Mark to solve a math problem. Mark doesn't have AI solve it; he tells AI to play tutor: no answers, just hints step by step and questions back. Fifteen minutes later, she finds the answer herself and can even explain it back to Uncle Mark.
Looking back on the day

Ten p.m., Mark looks at his tally: AI helped with ten tasks, and all ten final decisions were Mark's, so Bit stands up and claps because he didn't have to remind him once today. That's what three hundred videos have been saying: AI works fast, and you're the one at the wheel.
